Why Finomena is different

Agents that reason, act and check their own work.

Standard finance software follows a fixed path and stops at every exception. Finomena's agents work each case through, explain what they did, and ask a person only when it matters.

Agentic loops, not fixed workflows

Agents read the document or ledger, decide how to handle it, check the result and explain why. New formats are worked out on first sight.

Memory that compounds

Every correction and decision is kept as memory. The same exception is handled automatically next time, so value rises and cost falls each month.

Humans in the loop, by design

When an agent is unsure, a person gets the document, the evidence and a suggested action. You choose which steps always need a person.

No tool replacement

Runs on the SAP and Tally exports, Excel sheets and PDFs your team already uses. Nothing to rip out on day one.

    Myth-busting

    Six reasons teams hold off on automating AP, and why they no longer apply.

    THE MYTHTools only offer partial automation.

    Busted. Agents run the whole journey, receipt to posting. People step in for exceptions and approvals, not data entry.

    THE MYTHImplementation takes 3 to 6 months.

    Busted. It's configuration, not coding, so you go live in weeks. New rules go live in minutes.

    THE MYTHMaintenance and customisation cost a fortune.

    Busted. You change rules yourself, in plain English. No consultants and no change-request queue.

    THE MYTHAPI integration is slow and complex.

    Busted. Inputs and outputs, from email to SAP, are chosen by configuration instead of a months-long API build.

    THE MYTHAutomating the whole workflow is risky.

    Busted. Dial automation up or down per step. Start assisted and go touchless as trust builds.

    THE MYTHWe have too many exceptions for a standard tool.

    Busted. Build as many exception flows as you need. Every decision becomes memory, so the same question rarely comes back.

      Myth-busting

      Six reasons teams still reconcile in Excel, and why they no longer apply.

      THE MYTHYou can't automate when the two sides use different systems.

      Busted. Auto Recon reads SAP, Tally, Excel and PDF statements and works out how the two books map, from what the columns actually hold.

      THE MYTHEvery vendor needs a template built by IT.

      Busted. Agents design the plan on first sight. A reviewer corrects it in plain words, and it is saved for that vendor.

      THE MYTHOnly exact one-to-one matches can be automated.

      Busted. TDS, lump-sum payments, split invoices, timing and internal postings are matched or explained, and lines still reconcile only when the amounts agree.

      THE MYTHScanned statements mean retyping them.

      Busted. PDFs and photos are read page by page into a table you can download and check against the original.

      THE MYTHAutomation will hide differences.

      Busted. Nothing is forced. Every match shows why, every open item gets a reason and an action, and the statement ends at ₹0 unexplained.

      THE MYTHIt only pays off for the biggest vendors.

      Busted. Each vendor's plan is reused every period at near-zero cost, so every vendor can be reconciled, not just the top ten.

      What Auto Recon does

      From two ledgers to a signed-off statement.

      Five steps. Agents do the reading and matching; your team decides on the open items.

      01

      Read both books

      Our ledger and the vendor's, one sheet or many, Excel, CSV, PDF or a photo.

      02

      Design the plan

      Agents work out what each column holds, the signs, document types and TDS, and say what they are unsure of.

      03

      Match in passes

      Reference, cleaned reference, payments, TDS entries and combinations. A line is used once.

      04

      Explain the rest

      Every open item gets a reason and an action: missing, timing, amount or tax difference.

      05

      Sign off and share

      Manager sign-off, an Excel workbook and an email draft to the vendor with the open items.

      Built for how vendor ledgers really look

      The cases that make reconciliation slow, handled.

      TDS-aware matching

      Invoices booked net of TDS match the vendor's gross invoice and their TDS entry, including lump TDS journals and receipts grossed up by TDS.

      One against many

      A lump-sum payment against several receipts, a split invoice, a month of payments: one-to-many and many-to-one matches.

      Internal postings set aside

      Advance transfers, clearing pairs and reversed invoices that net to zero in one book are recognised, not reported as open.

      PDF and scanned statements

      Statements sent as PDFs or photos are read page by page into a table you can download and check.

      Tell the agent

      Ask why a line is open, or say what to match. The agent acts, but only on lines whose amounts agree.

      Learns each vendor

      The plan and every correction are saved per vendor, so the next period starts where this one ended.

        Where credit leaks

        Six places input tax credit quietly leaks, and how Auto GST catches each.

        Credit rarely goes missing as one big number. It leaks a few invoices at a time, in the same six places. Read the full guide →

        THE LEAKInvoices the supplier never reported, or reported against another of your GSTINs.

        Caught. Every invoice only in your books is listed by supplier, with the credit at stake and, for the largest, whether they have filed for that month, so you know whom to chase first.

        THE LEAKThe 30 November time limit under section 16(4).

        Caught. Invoices past the limit are marked time-barred, paired or not, and credit still at risk is shown before the deadline, largest first.

        THE LEAKBlocked credit under section 17(5) taken by default.

        Caught. Finomena AI flags likely blocked credit from the supplier, the line text, the ledger account and what your business does. A person confirms; a supplier you clear isn't flagged again.

        THE LEAKThe same invoice booked twice, then chased as missing.

        Caught. A second copy in your books is called out as booked twice, so the books get fixed and the supplier isn't chased for an invoice they already reported.

        THE LEAKCredit the 2B itself marks as not available.

        Caught. Lines GSTR-2B marks as not available are held apart as blocked and kept out of what you can claim.

        THE LEAKSmall differences nobody looks at: tax type, rate, our GSTIN.

        Caught. Every field is compared: GSTINs, number, date, taxable value, IGST, CGST, SGST and cess. IGST against CGST + SGST, and a different GSTIN of ours, are always checked.

        What Auto GST does

        From two files to a signed-off claim.

        Five steps. Code does the pairing and the arithmetic, Finomena AI handles what rules miss, and your team decides.

        01

        Read

        GSTR-2B as downloaded from the GST portal, and your purchase register in whatever layout your ERP exports. A new layout is learned once.

        02

        Pair

        Same supplier and invoice number, with separators and leading zeros set aside. Finomena AI proposes pairs for what is left; amounts must agree.

        03

        Explain

        Every difference shown with both sides and the amount that differs. Time limit, blocked credit and invoices booked twice are flagged.

        04

        Decide

        Claim, hold or ineligible, with a reason, for one pair or a whole group with the same difference. Decisions can be kept for next month.

        05

        Sign off

        A summary per GSTIN, suppliers to chase, changes since last month and a memo for the CFO. Signed off once every pair has a decision.

        Built for how 2B really looks

        The cases that make GSTR-2B slow, handled.

        Numbers written differently

        "INV/0123" and "123" pair up. When a person confirms one, the same pattern is learned for that supplier.

        Decide by group

        See the pairs with the same difference together, check them, then decide them in one go.

        Suppliers to chase

        Credit at risk by supplier, whether the largest have filed, and a reminder email drafted on request.

        Blocked credit, explained

        Each flag says why: the supplier, the line and the rule in section 17(5), including its exceptions.

        Nothing you did is lost

        Re-run with a corrected file and every decision and hand-made pair stays. Anything can be undone.

        Ready for the auditor

        Download in Excel: the summary, suppliers at risk and every line with its decision and reason.

        Home / About us About us

        We're building the finance back office that runs itself.

        Machines take over the mechanical. People still own the meaningful.

        In most companies, finance operations still run on people copying numbers from one screen to another. Invoices are keyed in by hand. Matching happens in spreadsheets. Vendors and colleagues are chased over email. Month-end becomes a marathon.

        The cost shows up everywhere: invoices that take more than a day to process, MSME vendors paid late, GST mismatches found too late to fix, and skilled people stuck doing data entry.

        Finomena exists to change that. We build AI products that do the repetitive work end to end and hand people only the decisions that need them. Large language models finally make this possible: software can now read messy documents, follow rules written in plain English, and learn an organisation's edge cases.

        Our mission

        Finance that runs itself, with people in charge of what matters.

        At Finomena, we believe finance teams should spend their time thinking, not processing. Our mission is to run finance operations with AI agents that do the mechanical work of receiving, checking, matching, posting and reconciling, and hand people only the judgement, analysis and decisions. We make this possible in weeks, not years: finance leaders describe how their operations should run in plain English, and Finomena turns those instructions into a working, autonomous programme. No code, no long implementations, no armies of consultants. Just finance that runs itself, with people in charge of what matters.

        GST · Input tax credit
        
        Six places input tax credit quietly leaks, and the monthly routine that catches them
        
        
        8 November 2026 · 6 min read
        
      
        
    
        
    
        
      
        
        
        Most finance teams match the purchase register to GSTR-2B once a month, in a spreadsheet, close to the filing date. The credit that slips through rarely shows up as one big number. It leaks a few invoices at a time, in six predictable places.
        

        
        1. Invoices your supplier never reported
        
        
        You can take credit only for invoices that appear in your GSTR-2B (section 16(2)(aa)). If a supplier files GSTR-1 late, reports the invoice under the wrong GSTIN, or does not report it at all, the credit is not available to you, even though you paid the full invoice including tax. Companies with several registrations see a variant of this: the supplier reports the invoice against another of your GSTINs, so the credit lands in the wrong state.
        
        
        Catch it: every month, list the booked invoices missing from 2B, grouped by supplier, and send each supplier one reminder with all their invoice numbers.
        

        
        2. The 30 November time limit
        
        
        Under section 16(4), credit for a financial year's invoices can be taken only until 30 November of the following year, or the date you file the annual return if that is earlier. For FY 2025-26 invoices the date is 30 November 2026. An invoice still missing from 2B after that date stays lost, even if the supplier reports it later.
        
        
        Catch it: in October and November, sort the missing-from-2B list by tax amount and chase the largest suppliers first.
        

        
        3. Invoices unpaid for more than 180 days
        
        
        If you do not pay a supplier the invoice value and tax within 180 days of the invoice date, the credit you took must be added back to your tax liability, with interest. You can take it again once you pay. Disputed and on-hold invoices are where this hides, because nobody is looking at them.
        
        
        Catch it: each month, list invoices where credit has been taken, payment is still open and the 180 days are close.
        

        
        4. Blocked credits booked as eligible
        
        
        Section 17(5) blocks credit on items such as food and beverages, club memberships, gifts, most motor vehicles, and construction of a building on your own account, each with specific exceptions. When these sit in a general expense ledger, the credit is often taken by default and then reversed, with interest, when the auditor finds it.
        
        
        Catch it: check the description of what was bought, not just the expense ledger it was posted to.
        

        
        5. The same invoice booked twice
        
        
        Duplicates come from re-sent PDFs, an email copy and a courier copy, or invoice numbers written differently ("INV/123" and "INV-0123"). Your 2B shows the invoice once; your books show it twice. Worse, the second copy appears as "missing from 2B", and the team chases a supplier who already reported it.
        
        
        Catch it: match on supplier GSTIN, invoice number with punctuation and leading zeros ignored, date and amount, not on the exact invoice number alone. Fix duplicates in the books instead of chasing the supplier.
        

        
        6. Credit the 2B itself marks as not available
        
        
        GSTR-2B lists some invoices as "ITC not available", for example where the place of supply makes the transaction ineligible for your registration, or where the section 16(4) time limit has passed. These are easy to sweep into the claim when the 2B is read as one total.
        
        
        Catch it: read the not-available section separately and keep those invoices out of the claim.
        

        
        Why this matters more now
        
        
        The GST network compares the credit you claim in GSTR-3B with your GSTR-2B. When the excess crosses a set threshold, it sends an intimation (DRC-01C) asking you to pay or explain. And with the Invoice Management System, invoices you take no action on are treated as accepted when your 2B is generated. Reviewing supplier invoices before the cut-off now matters as much as matching afterwards.
        

        
        A monthly routine that catches all six
        
        
          
          
        1. Match the purchase register to 2B invoice by invoice, allowing for rounding and different ways of writing invoice numbers.
          2. 
          
        2. Sort what is left into: missing from 2B (chase the supplier), in 2B but not in the books (check and book), and booked twice (fix the books).
          3. 
          
        3. Check blocked-credit purchases and 2B's not-available section before you claim.
          4. 
          
        4. Watch the 180-day payment clock and the 30 November time limit.
          5. 
          
        5. Record what was decided on each difference and why. Your auditor will ask.
          6. 
        
        

        
        Auto GST runs this routine every month: it pairs your purchase register with GSTR-2B for every GSTIN, explains each difference, flags blocked and time-barred credit, and lists the suppliers to chase.

        Home / Insights / Payables
        Payables · MSME
        
        MSME payments and section 43B(h): avoiding the year-end surprise
        
        
        8 November 2026 · 5 min read
        
      
        
    
        
    
        
      
        
        
        Since FY 2023-24, paying a micro or small supplier late does more than earn you an unhappy vendor. It can move a genuine expense out of the year you incurred it, and the extra tax shows up at year-end, when it is too late to fix.
        

        
        What the rule says
        
        
        Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act allows a deduction for amounts owed to micro and small enterprises in the year they are incurred only if they are paid within the time set by section 15 of the MSMED Act: by the agreed date, but not more than 45 days from accepting the goods or services, or within 15 days where there is no written agreement. Pay later, and the expense is deductible only in the year you actually pay.
        
        
        On top of that, the MSMED Act charges interest on late payments, compounded monthly at three times the bank rate notified by the RBI, and that interest is not deductible at all.
        

        
        Who it covers
        
        
        Micro and small enterprises registered on Udyam. Medium enterprises are outside it. Traders' registrations are widely treated as outside it too; confirm with your adviser. What counts is the supplier's status when you buy, so a classification captured once at onboarding can go stale.
        

        
        Where it goes wrong
        
        
          
          
        • The vendor master doesn't know. MSME status is missing, out of date, or recorded without the micro, small or medium classification.
          • 
          
        • Payment terms longer than the law allows. A 60- or 90-day term in the PO doesn't extend the 45-day limit.
          • 
          
        • The clock starts at acceptance, not at posting. An invoice that sits in someone's inbox or an approval queue for three weeks has used half its time before AP sees it.
          • 
          
        • Disputes left open. Held invoices quietly pass their due date.
          • 
        
        

        
        Reporting that depends on it
        
        
        Companies with dues to micro and small suppliers outstanding for more than 45 days file MSME Form I with the MCA every half-year, and the tax audit report asks for these amounts too. Both are hard to prepare without the due date of every invoice.
        

        
        A weekly routine that prevents it
        
        
          
          
        1. Capture the Udyam number and classification when a vendor is onboarded, and re-check them every year.
          2. 
          
        2. Work out each invoice's due date from the date the goods or services were accepted, not the posting date.
          3. 
          
        3. Every week, list MSME invoices due in the next seven days and those already overdue, and put them first in the payment run.
          4. 
          
        4. Before 31 March, list everything that will be disallowed if it stays unpaid, so the CFO can decide while there is still time.
          5. 
        
        

        
        Auto Invoice flags MSME invoices as they arrive, routes them by your own rules and predicts which ones are at risk of being paid late.

        Reconciliation
        
        Vendor reconciliation: the seven differences behind almost every gap
        
        
        8 November 2026 · 5 min read
        
      
        
    
        
    
        
      
        
        
        The vendor's statement says you owe one amount; your ledger says another. Teams often spend days on this line by line. In practice nearly every gap comes down to seven kinds of difference, and working through them in order makes the gap explain itself.
        

        
        The seven differences
        
        
          
          
        1. TDS. You deducted tax at source; the vendor hasn't recorded it yet, or records it only when it appears in their Form 26AS.
          2. 
          
        2. Invoices in transit. The vendor has billed; you haven't received the invoice, or it is waiting for approval.
          3. 
          
        3. Payments in transit. You paid on the 30th; the vendor recorded it on the 2nd.
          4. 
          
        4. Debit and credit notes. Rate differences, short supplies or discounts recorded by only one side.
          5. 
          
        5. Duplicates and reversals. The same invoice posted twice, or reversed on one side only.
          6. 
          
        6. The opening balance. A difference from an earlier period that was never agreed, carried forward every time.
          7. 
          
        7. The wrong account. A payment posted to a sister vendor code, or to another entity of the same vendor group.
          8. 
        
        

        
        Why spreadsheets struggle
        
        
        Statements arrive as PDFs, Tally exports and scanned pages, each laid out differently. One payment often settles five invoices. The vendor's debit is your credit, so signs flip. And a reconciliation done once is rarely saved in a form you can reuse next quarter, so the next one starts from scratch.
        

        
        A routine that works
        
        
          
          
        1. Reconcile the largest and most critical vendors monthly and the rest quarterly.
          2. 
          
        2. Start from the last balance both sides agreed, not from the start of the year.
          3. 
          
        3. Match exact amounts first, then one payment against several invoices, then the rest.
          4. 
          
        4. Put every open item into one of the seven differences. Anything that doesn't fit is the one that needs a person.
          5. 
          
        5. Send the vendor one email listing exactly what you need from them.
          6.
